::: {.notes}
Welcome to Parse, Don't Pray. Inspired by Alexis King's essay on parsing, this talk examines how Pydantic in Python and Zod in TypeScript can turn external input into data that the rest of a program can use with clearer expectations.
:::

## What You'll Learn {.smaller}

- Why data validation libraries are essential for robust applications
- Why validation is needed on **both** client and server (not just one)
- How Pydantic (Python) and Zod (TypeScript) improve code quality
- Benefits across readability, runtime behaviour, typing, testing, and security

::: {style="background-color: #FFFBC1; padding: 20px; border-radius: 25px; text-align: center;"}

🎯 **Goal**

Create a **validated type system** that works at runtime, ensuring data actually matches your assumptions.

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e3f2fd; padding: 20px; border-radius: 25px; text-align: center;"}

Examples assume a **Python-TypeScript** full-stack, but the principles apply to other stacks.

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; margin-top: 8px;"}
Python: [`pydantic[email]`](https://pypi.org/project/pydantic/); currency: [`pydantic-extra-types`](https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-extra-types/) + [`pycountry`](https://pypi.org/project/pycountry/); tests: [pytest](https://pypi.org/project/pytest/) / [Vitest](https://www.npmjs.com/package/vitest).
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
We will look at the gap between static types and runtime input, then at readability, parsing behaviour, errors, and type inference. We will also discuss testing, security boundaries, and sharing contracts across a system. The package links below the goal lead to the dependencies used in the examples.
:::

# Introduction

*Why data validation matters*

::: {.notes}
A system has to interact with data it did not create. A boundary is where the assumptions inside our program meet input from somewhere else.
:::

## Dynamic vs Static Typing {.smaller}

Type systems differ in **when** they catch type errors.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 0.85em;"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; font-weight: bold; margin-bottom: 8px;"}
**Statically Typed** (e.g., Java, C++, Rust)
:::

- Types checked at **compile time**
- Type errors caught before runtime
- Type inference can reduce declarations
- Guarantees have language-specific limits

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
```rust
fn greet(name: String) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {}!", name)
}

// Won't compile: type mismatch
greet(42);  // Error at compile time
```
:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

::: {style="background-color: #fff3e0; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 0.85em;"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; font-weight: bold; margin-bottom: 8px;"}
**Dynamically Typed** (e.g., Python, JavaScript)
:::

- Types checked at **runtime**
- Type errors appear during execution
- More flexible, less verbose
- No compile-time type guarantees

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
```python
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name.upper()}!"

# Works with correct type
greet("alice")  # "Hello, ALICE!"
# Wrong type fails at runtime
greet(42)       # Runtime error: 'int' object has no attribute 'upper'
```
:::

:::

:::

::::

. . .

::: {style="background-color: #e3f2fd; padding: 10px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 10px; text-align: center; font-size: 0.9em;"}

**Every language needs boundary checks**: static types alone do not validate incoming data.

:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [TypeScript type erasure](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/basic-types.html#erased-types)
:::

::: {.notes}
A static type annotation does not establish that an incoming payload has the expected shape. TypeScript types are erased, and Python does not automatically enforce its annotations. Runtime parsing provides the check that a type declaration alone cannot perform on external data.
:::

## What is Data Validation? {.smaller}

Ensuring data meets specific criteria before use.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

::: {style="background-color: #ffebee; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 0.85em;"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; font-weight: bold; margin-bottom: 8px;"}
**❌ Without validation libraries**
:::

Manual checks scattered throughout code:

- Type, range, and format checks written by hand
- Logic spreads across codebase
- Difficult to maintain and extend

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 0.85em;"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; font-weight: bold; margin-bottom: 8px;"}
**✅ With validation libraries**
:::

Schemas validate and parse inputs into typed outputs:

- Centralised, self-documenting rules
- Explicit coercion where appropriate
- Detailed error messages
- Easier to maintain and evolve

:::

:::

::::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic models](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/) · [Zod parsing](https://zod.dev/basics)
:::

::: {.notes}
At a boundary, validation checks whether input has the expected structure, types, and constraints. That is distinct from later decisions such as whether an account has enough funds for a transaction. Both are useful, but they answer different questions.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pydantic builds models around Python's type hints. Zod provides composable runtime schemas that can also inform TypeScript's static types. Both let a developer state an input contract explicitly instead of scattering checks throughout the program.
:::

# Benefits of Data Validation Libraries

*Creating robust, maintainable applications*

::: {.notes}
Let’s look at what those explicit schemas change in everyday code, starting with readability.
:::

# Readability

*Self-documenting schemas that reduce cognitive load*

::: {.notes}
A schema puts the accepted shape of the data in one place. That makes the contract easier to see than a collection of checks spread through the implementation.
:::

## Self-Documenting Schemas {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field
from typing import Annotated, Literal

UserName = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)]

class UserProfile(BaseModel):
    username: UserName
    email: EmailStr
    age: int = Field(ge=18, le=120)
    role: Literal["admin", "user", "guest"]
    is_active: bool = True
```

### TypeScript (Zod)

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const UserName = z.string().min(3).max(20);

const UserProfileSchema = z.object({
  username: UserName,
  email: z.email(),
  age: z.int().min(18).max(120),
  role: z.enum(["admin", "user", "guest"]),
  isActive: z.boolean().default(true),
});

type UserProfile = z.infer<typeof UserProfileSchema>;
```

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e3f2fd; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 10px; text-align: center;"}
Rules and type information stay synchronised; explain intent in human-facing docs.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic fields](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/fields/) · [Zod schemas](https://zod.dev/api)
:::

::: {.notes}
Nested conditions and repeated key checks can obscure the operation a function is meant to perform. A declarative model makes the expected fields and constraints easier to inspect, leaving the main operation less cluttered.
:::

## Specific Types Over Generic {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="24%"}

::: {style="background-color: #ffebee; padding: 10px; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.9em;"}

**❌ Generic: `str`**

```python
class User(BaseModel):
    email: str
```

- Accepts any string
- No email-format check
- Unclear intent

:::

:::

::: {.column width="38%"}

::: {style="background-color: #fff3e0; padding: 10px; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.9em;"}

**⚠️ Better: `EmailStr`**

```python
class User(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
```

- Validates email format
- Self-documenting
- Still generic

:::

:::

::: {.column width="38%"}

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 10px; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.9em;"}

**✅ Domain rule**

```python
from pydantic import AfterValidator, BaseModel, EmailStr
from typing import Annotated

def must_be_acme(value: str) -> str:
    if not value.endswith('@acme.com'):
        raise ValueError('Must be @acme.com')
    return value

AcmeEmailStr = Annotated[
    EmailStr,
    AfterValidator(must_be_acme),
]

class User(BaseModel):
    email: AcmeEmailStr
```

- Domain-specific
- Business rule enforced
- Crystal clear intent

:::

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="24%"}

::: {style="background-color: #ffebee; padding: 10px; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.9em;"}

**❌ Generic: `string`**

```typescript
const UserSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string(),
});
```

- Accepts any string
- No email-format check
- Unclear intent

:::

:::

::: {.column width="38%"}

::: {style="background-color: #fff3e0; padding: 10px; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.9em;"}

**⚠️ Better: `z.email()`**

```typescript
const UserSchema = z.object({
  email: z.email(),
});
```

- Validates email format
- Self-documenting
- Still generic

:::

:::

::: {.column width="38%"}

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 10px; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.9em;"}

**✅ Domain rule**

```typescript
const acmeEmail = z.email()
  .refine(
    (email) => email.endsWith('@acme.com'),
    { error: 'Must be @acme.com email' }
  );

const UserSchema = z.object({
  email: acmeEmail,
});
```

- Domain-specific
- Business rule enforced
- Crystal clear intent

:::

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e3f2fd; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Choose the constraints your domain needs; email format does not prove mailbox ownership.
:::

:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic email types](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/networks/#pydantic.networks.EmailStr) · [Zod refinements](https://zod.dev/api#refinements)
:::

::: {.notes}
A generic string or integer often permits more values than the domain expects. A field for an email address or a positive quantity can state that constraint directly. The resulting parser checks those requirements before returning the accepted value.
:::

# Runtime Behaviour

*Catch errors early before they propagate*

::: {.notes}
At runtime, the schema becomes an active boundary: it accepts, transforms, or rejects input according to the rules we have defined.
:::

## Automatic Validation {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, PositiveFloat
from pydantic_extra_types.currency_code import Currency

class ProductPrice(BaseModel):
    product_id: str
    price: PositiveFloat
    currency: Currency
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Validation Examples**

```python
# ✅ Valid data passes through
ProductPrice(
    product_id="PROD-123",
    price=29.99,
    currency="USD"
)

# 🚫 Invalid data blocked
ProductPrice(
    product_id="PROD-123",
    price=-10,     # Negative!
    currency="US"  # Invalid format!
)
```

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const ProductPriceSchema = z.object({
  productId: z.string(),
  price: z.number().positive(),
  currency: z.currencyCode(),
});
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Validation Examples**

```typescript
// ✅ Valid data passes through
ProductPriceSchema.parse({
  productId: "PROD-123",
  price: 29.99,
  currency: "USD",
});

// 🚫 Invalid data blocked
ProductPriceSchema.parse({
  productId: "PROD-123",
  price: -10,     // Negative!
  currency: "US", // Invalid format!
});
```

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Data validated as it enters the system, catching errors early.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic currency](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/pydantic_extra_types_currency_code/) · [Zod currency](https://zod.dev/api#currency-codes)
:::

::: {.notes}
Failing at the boundary makes an invalid input easier to diagnose. Instead of letting it travel deeper into the system, the parser can reject it before later code relies on an assumption that does not hold.
:::

## Data Coercion & Parsing {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from datetime import datetime

class Event(BaseModel):
    event_id: int        # Coerces string to int
    timestamp: datetime  # Parses ISO 8601 strings
    is_public: bool      # Coerces to bool
    attendees: list[str] # Coerces tuple to list
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Coercion Examples**

```python
event = Event(
    event_id="42",                    # → int 42
    timestamp="2024-01-15T10:30:00",  # → datetime
    is_public="yes",                  # → True
    attendees=("Alice", "Bob")        # → list
)
```

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```{.typescript code-line-numbers="4,5"}
import { z } from "zod";

const EventSchema = z.object({
  eventId: z.string().regex(/^\d+$/)
    .pipe(z.coerce.number()).pipe(z.int()),
  timestamp: z.coerce.date(),
  isPublic: z.stringbool(),
  attendees: z.array(z.string()),
});
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Coercion Examples**

```typescript
const event = EventSchema.parse({
  eventId: "42",                     // → number 42
  timestamp: "2024-01-15T10:30:00",  // → Date
  isPublic: "yes",                   // → boolean true
  attendees: ["Alice", "Bob"],
});
```

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e3f2fd; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Pydantic coerces by default; Zod requires opt-in.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic conversions](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/conversion_table/) · [Zod coercion](https://zod.dev/api#coercion)
:::

::: {.notes}
Parsing can do more than answer yes or no. It can turn a date string into a date object or another external representation into the type the program expects. The accepted transformations must be deliberate, particularly when coercion would hide an input error. Keep using the parsed model or object returned by the library; checking validity alone does not transform the original input.
:::

## Detailed Error Messages {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field

class SignupForm(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3)
    email: EmailStr
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Error Messages**

```python
from pydantic import ValidationError

try:
    user = SignupForm(
        username="ab",        # Too short
        email="not-an-email", # Invalid format
    )
except ValidationError as e:
    issues = [
        {"loc": err["loc"], "msg": err["msg"]}
        for err in e.errors()
    ]
    print(issues)  # Two field errors
```

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const SignupFormSchema = z.object({
  username: z.string().min(3),
  email: z.email(),
});
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Error Messages**

```typescript
const result = SignupFormSchema.safeParse({
  username: "ab",            // Too short
  email: "not-an-email",     // Invalid format
});

if (!result.success) {
  console.log(z.treeifyError(result.error));
  // Abbreviated: root properties
  // {
  //   "username": { "errors": ["Too small: ..."] },
  //   "email": { "errors": ["Invalid email address"] }
  // }
}
```

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #fff3e0; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Map structured errors to fields; avoid exposing raw input or secrets in logs and responses.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic errors](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/errors/errors/) · [Zod error formatting](https://zod.dev/error-formatting)
:::

::: {.notes}
Structured errors identify which field failed and why. That helps an API client correct a request and lets an interface associate feedback with the relevant form field. It is more useful than discovering an unrelated exception much later in processing.
:::

# Typing

*Type inference that bridges static and runtime worlds*

::: {.notes}
Runtime schemas and static typing can support each other. The aim is to avoid maintaining two separate descriptions of the same contract.
:::

## Type Inference {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str

user = User(name="Alice")
name = user.name  # Inferred as str by type checkers
```

The field annotation supplies the type; no separate type for `name` is needed.

### TypeScript (Zod)

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const UserSchema = z.object({ name: z.string() });
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>; // { name: string }

const user = UserSchema.parse({ name: "Alice" });
const name = user.name;  // Inferred as string
```

`z.infer` describes parsed output; `z.input` describes accepted input.

:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic models](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/) · [Zod input and output types](https://zod.dev/basics#inferring-types)
:::

::: {.notes}
One field is enough to see the relationship. In Python, the model declares name as a string, so a type checker knows that reading user.name produces a string. In TypeScript, Zod's infer utility derives the User type from the runtime schema, and the parsed object's name is also known to be a string. Zod distinguishes its input and output types when a parser transforms values; infer refers to the output. Neither example needs a second handwritten description of the user's fields.
:::

## End-to-End Type Safety {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Literal

class ApiResponse(BaseModel):
    status: Literal["success", "error"]
    data: list[dict]
    message: str
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Type-Safe Usage**

```python
def fetch_data_from_api() -> ApiResponse:
    raw_response = requests.get(
        "https://api.example.com/data"
    ).json()
    return ApiResponse.model_validate(raw_response)

def process_response(response: ApiResponse) -> None:
    if response.status == "success":
        for item in response.data:
            process_item(item)

response = fetch_data_from_api()
process_response(response)
```

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const ApiResponseSchema = z.object({
  status: z.enum(["success", "error"]),
  data: z.array(z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())),
  message: z.string(),
});

type ApiResponse = z.infer<typeof ApiResponseSchema>;
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Type-Safe Usage**

```typescript
async function fetchDataFromApi(): Promise<ApiResponse> {
  const rawResponse = await fetch(
    "https://api.example.com/data"
  );
  const json = await rawResponse.json();
  return ApiResponseSchema.parse(json);
}

function processResponse(response: ApiResponse): void {
  if (response.status === "success") {
    for (const item of response.data) {
      processItem(item);
    }
  }
}
```

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e3f2fd; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
External data is validated before entering your type-safe code!
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic model validation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/#validating-data) · [Zod parsing](https://zod.dev/basics#parsing-data)
:::

::: {.notes}
Shared schemas and generated clients can connect contracts across a system. When a contract changes, the affected types and generated code must be updated too. That gives type checking a chance to reveal incompatibilities before the changed request reaches production.
:::

# Testing

*Verify your contract and integrations*

::: {.notes}
A clear parsing boundary also changes how we organise tests. We can concentrate input-contract tests where the contract is enforced.
:::

## Test the Contract You Own {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

```python
import pytest
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

class Signup(BaseModel):
    age: int = Field(ge=18)

def test_adult_signup_boundary():
    Signup(age=18)  # Our policy accepts this age
    with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
        Signup(age=17)
```

### TypeScript (Zod)

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";
import { expect, it } from "vitest";

const SignupSchema = z.object({ age: z.int().min(18) });

it("accepts adults and rejects underage signups", () => {
  expect(SignupSchema.safeParse({ age: 18 }).success).toBe(true);
  expect(SignupSchema.safeParse({ age: 17 }).success).toBe(false);
});
```

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Test your chosen rules and error handling; avoid repeating the library's own type-validation tests.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic validation errors](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/errors/errors/) · [Zod safeParse](https://zod.dev/basics#handling-errors)
:::

::: {.notes}
The rule we own here is that adult signups start at eighteen. Testing that eighteen is accepted and seventeen is rejected protects that policy against accidentally changing or removing the minimum. We do not need to assert that the model stores the age we supplied, or repeat the library's tests for every invalid integer representation. Add tests for custom rules and for how the application handles a rejected signup.
:::

# Security

*Constrain untrusted input before business logic*

::: {.notes}
Validation is also part of the security boundary. It makes accepted input explicit, although other protections are still needed for how that data is used.
:::

## Reject Unexpected Fields {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```{.python code-line-numbers="4"}
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')
    email: str
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Mass Assignment Prevention**

```python
# ✅ Safe request
UserUpdate(email="user@example.com")

# 🚫 Malicious fields blocked
UserUpdate(
    email="hacker@evil.com",
    is_admin=True,   # Attack!
    balance=999999,  # Attack!
)
```

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```{.typescript code-line-numbers="3"}
import { z } from "zod";

const UserUpdateSchema = z.strictObject({
  email: z.email(),
});
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Mass Assignment Prevention**

```typescript
// ✅ Safe request
UserUpdateSchema.parse({ email: "user@example.com" });

// 🚫 Malicious fields blocked
UserUpdateSchema.parse({
  email: "hacker@evil.com",
  isAdmin: true,    // Attack!
  balance: 999999,  // Attack!
});
```

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #ffebee; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Rejecting unknown fields blocks one mass-assignment path; authorisation is still required.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic extra fields](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/#extra-data) · [Zod strictObject](https://zod.dev/api#zstrictobject)
:::

::: {.notes}
Unexpected fields can be dangerous when a payload is applied directly to an internal object. A request might try to set an administrative flag or a tenant identifier. Rejecting fields outside the accepted schema helps keep that input contract narrow.
:::

## Type Confusion Prevention {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, PositiveFloat
from pydantic_extra_types.currency_code import Currency

class PaymentRequest(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)

    user_id: str
    amount: PositiveFloat
    currency: Currency
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Type Confusion Prevention**

```python
# 🚫 String instead of float blocked
PaymentRequest(
    user_id="USR-123",
    amount="0.01 OR 1=1",  # Attack!
    currency="USD"
)

# 🚫 Array instead of string blocked
PaymentRequest(
    user_id=["USR-123", "ADMIN"],  # Attack!
    amount=10.0,
    currency="USD"
)
```

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const PaymentRequestSchema = z.object({
  userId: z.string(),
  amount: z.number().positive(),
  currency: z.currencyCode(),
});
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Type Confusion Prevention**

```typescript
// 🚫 String instead of number blocked
PaymentRequestSchema.parse({
  userId: "USR-123",
  amount: "0.01 OR 1=1",  // Attack!
  currency: "USD",
});

// 🚫 Array instead of string blocked
PaymentRequestSchema.parse({
  userId: ["USR-123", "ADMIN"],  // Attack!
  amount: 10.0,
  currency: "USD",
});
```

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #fff3e0; padding: 10px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 8px; text-align: center; font-size: 0.85em;"}
Strict types and unknown-field rejection are separate settings. Pydantic's strict JSON mode still accepts some strings, such as dates.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic strict mode](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/strict_mode/) · [Zod schemas](https://zod.dev/api)
:::

::: {.notes}
Type confusion occurs when an operation receives a different kind of value from the one it expects. Boundary checks can catch that mismatch early. Strict types do not reject extra keys: configure that separately. Pydantic also distinguishes Python input from JSON input in strict mode. Parameterised queries and safe command APIs remain necessary.
:::

## Size & Range Limits {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Annotated

class CommentSubmission(BaseModel):
    post_id: str
    author: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=50)
    content: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=5000)
    tags: list[Annotated[str, Field(max_length=30)]] = Field(max_length=10)
    rating: int = Field(ge=1, le=5)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Oversized Input Rejection**

```python
# 🚫 Massive content blocked
CommentSubmission(
    post_id="POST-123",
    author="attacker",
    content="X" * 1_000_000,  # 1MB!
    tags=["spam"] * 1000,     # 1000 tags!
    rating=999                # Out of range!
)
# Errors:
# - content: max 5000 characters
# - tags: max 10 items
# - rating: max 5
```

:::

::::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Schema Definition**

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const CommentSubmissionSchema = z.object({
  postId: z.string(),
  author: z.string().min(1).max(50),
  content: z.string().min(1).max(5000),
  tags: z.array(z.string().max(30)).max(10),
  rating: z.int().min(1).max(5),
});
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Oversized Input Rejection**

```typescript
// 🚫 Massive content blocked
CommentSubmissionSchema.parse({
  postId: "POST-123",
  author: "attacker",
  content: "X".repeat(1_000_000),  // 1MB!
  tags: Array(1000).fill("spam"),  // 1000 tags!
  rating: 999,                     // Out of range!
});
// Errors:
// - content: max 5000 character(s)
// - tags: max 10 element(s)
// - rating: max 5
```

:::

::::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #ffebee; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Schema limits bound downstream work; enforce request-size limits at the server or proxy too.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic fields](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/fields/) · [Zod constraints](https://zod.dev/api)
:::

::: {.notes}
Sizes and ranges belong in the input contract too. Very long strings, large arrays, or extreme numeric values can create expensive processing. Define the bounds the application actually needs, rather than accepting an unlimited input by default.
:::

# Full-Stack Validation

*Client + Server validation for UX and security*

::: {.notes}
A full-stack application has more than one place to check input. The browser and server have different responsibilities.
:::

## Why Both Sides Matter {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="background-color: #ffebee; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 0.75em;"}

**❌ Client-Only Validation**

```typescript
const UserSchema = z.object({
  role: z.enum(["user", "guest"]),
});
```

```bash
# Attacker bypasses frontend entirely
curl -X POST /api/users \
  -d '{"role": "admin"}'
```

Frontend never ran – attacker sends `"admin"` directly. A server that trusts this role could grant unauthorised privileges.

Client validation is for **UX** (fast feedback), not security.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="background-color: #fff3e0; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 0.75em;"}

**⚠️ Server-Only Validation**

```typescript
async function submit(data: unknown) {
  await fetch("/api/users", {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify(data),
  });
}
```

Without client-side checks, feedback needs a round trip. A poor server UI might reveal one error at a time:

1. Submit → "Email invalid" → fix → resubmit
2. "Age too low" → fix → resubmit
3. Finally succeeds after **3 round trips**

Enforce the contract on the server; add client checks for fast feedback, and return all useful field errors together.

:::

:::

::::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [OWASP input validation](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html)
:::

::: {.notes}
Client-side checks give a person quick feedback, but a request can reach the server without using that interface. The server must enforce its own input contract. The two layers can share rules while still serving these different purposes.
:::

# Additional Benefits

*More advantages of using validation libraries*

::: {.notes}
Schema-driven design also helps with documentation and configuration. The same explicit contracts can support tools beyond the immediate request handler.
:::

## API Design & Documentation {.smaller}

Framework integrations connect schemas to validation, types, **and** documentation.

::: {.schema-flow}

```{mermaid}
%%| eval: true
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 9
flowchart LR
    S["🔷 <b>Schema</b><br/><i>Pydantic / Zod</i>"]
    S --> V["✅ <b>Request &<br/>Response Validation</b>"]
    S --> T["🔒 <b>Type Safety</b><br/><i>IDE autocomplete</i>"]
    S --> D["📄 <b>OpenAPI / JSON Schema</b>"]
    D --> UI["🌐 <b>Interactive Docs</b><br/><i>/docs &bull; Swagger UI</i>"]
    D --> CG["⚙️ <b>Client Code<br/>Generation</b>"]

    style S fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,color:#0d47a1
    style V fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#1b5e20
    style T fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#1b5e20
    style D fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100,color:#bf360c
    style UI fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#c62828,color:#b71c1c
    style CG fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#c62828,color:#b71c1c
```

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
`Model.model_json_schema()` and `z.toJSONSchema(schema)` export contracts. Custom rules and transforms may not be representable; review generated output.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic JSON Schema](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/json_schema/) · [Zod JSON Schema](https://zod.dev/json-schema)
:::

::: {.notes}
Schemas can support API documentation and standard descriptions such as OpenAPI and JSON Schema. Those descriptions can then feed client generators and other tools. Keeping them connected to the implementation reduces the number of separate contracts to maintain. Review exported schemas because custom validators and transforms may not survive conversion. Frameworks connect JSON Schema to routes, OpenAPI, and interactive documentation.
:::

## Frozen Configs: Know the Limits {.smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python (Pydantic)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Mutable**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

class MutableConfig(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(validate_assignment=True)
    max_retries: int = Field(ge=1, le=10)

config = MutableConfig(max_retries=3)
config.max_retries = 5  # Accepted
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Frozen**

```python
class FrozenConfig(MutableConfig):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

config = FrozenConfig(max_retries=3)
config.max_retries = 5  # ValidationError
```

:::

::::

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; margin-top: 8px;"}
`validate_assignment=True` rechecks field reassignment on the mutable model.
:::

### TypeScript (Zod)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Mutable**

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const MutableSchema = z.object({
  maxRetries: z.int().min(1).max(10),
});

const mutable = MutableSchema.parse({ maxRetries: 3 });
mutable.maxRetries = 5;  // Accepted
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Frozen**

```typescript
const FrozenSchema = MutableSchema.readonly();

const frozen = FrozenSchema.parse({ maxRetries: 3 });
frozen.maxRetries = 5;  // TypeScript error
// Runtime TypeError if attempted in strict mode
```

:::

::::

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em; margin-top: 8px;"}
Zod validates when parsing; later mutations are not revalidated automatically.
:::

:::

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: center;"}
Freezing is shallow: choose immutable nested types when deep immutability matters.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic faux immutability](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/#faux-immutability) · [Zod readonly](https://zod.dev/api#readonly)
:::

::: {.notes}
The two columns use the same field and constraints so that the difference is visible. The mutable Pydantic model accepts a change from three retries to five, and assignment validation checks the new value. Its frozen subclass rejects field reassignment. Zod's parsed object is mutable by default, and later mutations do not run its schema again. Adding readonly returns a frozen object and a readonly TypeScript type. Both forms of freezing protect the top level only; nested mutable collections need their own protection. Separately, Pydantic defaults require validate_default to be checked, and Zod's prefault parses a fallback where default returns it directly.
:::

# Summary

*Creating a validated type system that works at runtime*

::: {.notes}
The central idea is to make assumptions explicit where data enters the program, then carry the parsed result forward through the system.
:::

## Key Takeaways {.smaller}

Data validation libraries like Pydantic and Zod transform how we build applications:

. . .

::: {style="background-color: #e8f5e9; padding: 20px; border-radius: 10px; margin: 15px 0;"}

**Readability**: Executable contracts that keep rules and types synchronised

**Runtime Safety**: Catch errors at system boundaries before they propagate

**Type Safety**: Bridge the gap between static types and runtime data

**Testing**: Focus tests on domain rules, boundaries, and failure handling

**Security**: Reject unexpected or oversized input before business logic

:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color: #FFFBC1; padding: 20px; border-radius: 25px; text-align: center; font-size: 1.1em; margin-top: 20px;"}

**Parse, don't pray!** Validate at boundaries, use parsed outputs, and preserve their invariants.

:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.55em; color: #666; margin-top: 10px;"}
Sources: [Pydantic models](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/) · [Zod parsing](https://zod.dev/basics)
:::

::: {.notes}
Use established parsing tools, define the fields and bounds you accept, and reject invalid input early. Connect runtime schemas to types and documentation where useful. The result is a clearer contract for both the implementation and its users.
:::
